newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin alone as he fights battle of his life.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin alone as he fights battle of his life.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin's decision to undergo heart surgery must have been all the harder with his old Kremlin allies gone, his wife in hospital and his energy reserves low after a draining re-election battle.
Judging by official reports of his movements since he dropped from public view in late June, Yeltsin has been spending reflective weeks in the seclusion of the Russian countryside.
A Kremlin source said he went fishing this week.

Few believed his aides' story that he was just tired, and the fleeting glimpses of Yeltsin in edited television pictures did little to dispel the impression that his ischaemic heart condition -- a blood supply problem -- needed attention.

The purpose of the Kremlin leader's vanishing act to Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow, the northwestern lakeland of Valdai and then the Rus hunting lodge close to the capital now seems clear -- he had been taking the decision of his life.

Facing four more years at the helm of the turbulent Russian federation, the 65-year-old leader looked almost relieved when he announced on Thursday that he had listened to his doctors and would go under the surgeon's scalpel at the end of this month.
But he made clear he was not planning to put his feet up despite resting since winning a second term on July 3 -- the surgery would allow him to lead an active life, he said.

British doctors said on Friday that Yeltsin, in choosing bypass surgery rather than a less complicated procedure to unblock arteries -- had taken the tougher of two options which could lead to a break of two to three months from work.
It can have been no easy move, even for the man who clambered atop a tank outside the White House to defy a hardline coup attempt against Mikhail Gorbachev in August 1991.
Then, Alexander Korzhakov, his broad-shouldered bodyguard, tennis partner, old friend and drinking buddy, stood behind him.
But Yeltsin was forced to oust Korzhakov from the Kremlin on June 20 amid allegations that the bull-like former KGB general was behind a suspected attempt to derail the election runoff.
Yeltsin's wife, Naina, said it had been a very tough decision not only for her husband but for the whole family. "It feels as if part of your body has been cut off," she said.
Another close ally and senior aide, Viktor Ilyushin, has also left the Kremlin to take up a post as one of three first deputy prime ministers as part of a post-election reshuffle.
Talk was once that Yeltsin paid more attention to Korzhakov than he did to his own wife.
But even Naina, 64, was not there to back him up as he decided to have surgery -- she had a kidney operation on August 24 and is not expected to leave hospital for several days.
Naina has always portrayed her husband as a self-starter who hates taking advice.
It seems she resorted to extreme measures to make him face up to his health problem. Ekho Moskvy radio said she had refused to have her operation until he had medical tests.
A day after he won a second term, she said she wished he would take a week or two off, or at least ease up on his 20-hour working day.
"I don't know what decision he will make, I can't say. It's very difficult to convince Boris Nikolayevich of anything. If he decides something it's almost impossible to stop him," she said.
But even Yeltsin had to stop and take care of himself. "He's not a superman," she said. "He's a man like everyone else".
